problem.title: Non-Blocking Async & Structured Logging
problem.prompt: A 20-pod Spring Boot order-ingestion service (200 Tomcat worker threads/pod, gp3 EBS 3,000 IOPS limit) enables verbose DEBUG/JSON request logging during an incident. At 1,800 RPS/pod, each request writes 6 log lines (~4.5 KB). With Logback's synchronous `FileAppender` (`immediateFlush=true`), disk queue depth hits 128 and write latency spikes to 45 ms per line—blocking all 200 worker threads in `FileOutputStream.writeBytes` and dropping throughput to near zero.
requirements: Decouple HTTP worker threads from disk I/O so request latency stays < 25 ms even if EBS stalls for 500 ms.
Handle 1,800 RPS/pod (10,800 log events/sec = ~8.1 MB/s) without exhausting JVM heap.
Ensure ERROR/FATAL logs are never silently dropped during normal operation, while gracefully shedding DEBUG/INFO if the disk falls behind.
Keep log-to-disk durability lag under 1 second during normal operation and flush cleanly on SIGTERM.
constraints: Logs must still be written to local `/var/log/app/app.log` for Fluent Bit DaemonSet tailing (cannot switch to direct network-only logging).
Node gp3 EBS volume is shared with containerd image layers and capped at 3,000 IOPS / 125 MB/s.
JVM heap is 4 GB; max memory dedicated to log buffering must be <= 64 MB.

stages.learnerPrompt: Why did enabling DEBUG logging cause all 200 Tomcat worker threads to block even though CPU was low?

referenceMaterial.summary: Synchronous FileAppender acquires a global lock around OutputStream.write() and flushes every line, turning EBS IOPS saturation into a 200-thread mutex pileup.
approachSteps: Show 1,800 RPS * 6 lines = 10,800 syscalls/sec per pod.
Explain how gp3 3,000 IOPS limit drives write latency to 45 ms/line.
Note that all 200 worker threads queue behind FileOutputStream.writeBytes.
referenceMaterial.codeSnippet:
<!-- Broken synchronous Logback config -->
<appender name="FILE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.RollingFileAppender">
  <file>/var/log/app/app.log</file>
  <immediateFlush>true</immediateFlush> <!-- Forces 10,800 flushes/sec on worker threads -->
</appender>
tradeOffs: immediateFlush=true guarantees each line hits the OS page cache immediately at the cost of destroying throughput.
alternatives: Writing to stdout (containerd json-file driver), which still hits the same node EBS volume.
failureModes: Complete service freeze whenever log verbosity increases or EBS bursts run out.

stages.learnerPrompt: Write the Log4j2 XML and JVM system properties to decouple worker threads, batch writes, and prevent blocking if the disk stalls.
Review the production Log4j2 AsyncLogger XML and Disruptor properties.

referenceMaterial.summary: Uses Log4j2 AsyncLoggerContextSelector with 65,536-slot ring buffer, Discard policy for INFO/DEBUG, and 256 KB buffered RollingFileAppender with immediateFlush=false.
approachSteps: Configure RollingFile with bufferSize=262144 and immediateFlush=false.
referenceMaterial.codeSnippet:
<!-- log4j2-spring.xml -->
<Configuration status="WARN">
  <Appenders>
    <RollingFile name="AppFile" fileName="/var/log/app/app.log"
                 filePattern="/var/log/app/app-%i.log"
                 bufferSize="262144" immediateFlush="false">
      <JsonTemplateLayout eventTemplateUri="classpath:EcsLayout.json"/>
      <Policies>
        <SizeBasedTriggeringPolicy size="100 MB"/>
      </Policies>
      <DefaultRolloverStrategy max="5"/>
    </RollingFile>
  </Appenders>
  <Loggers>
    <Root level="INFO">
      <AppenderRef ref="AppFile"/>
    </Root>
  </Loggers>
</Configuration>
<!-- JVM Flags:
-Dlog4j2.contextSelector=org.apache.logging.log4j.core.async.AsyncLoggerContextSelector
-Dlog4j2.asyncLoggerRingBufferSize=65536
-Dlog4j2.asyncQueueFullPolicy=Discard
-Dlog4j2.discardThreshold=INFO -->
tradeOffs: Using Discard drops INFO/DEBUG logs if disk stalls > 6s, prioritizing API availability over verbose logs.
alternatives: Logback AsyncAppender with neverBlock=true and discardingThreshold=20.
failureModes: Forgetting asyncQueueFullPolicy=Discard still blocks worker threads when the 65k ring fills.

stages.learnerPrompt: Why does `immediateFlush=false` in Log4j2 AsyncLogger not lose logs for minutes during normal operation?

referenceMaterial.summary: Log4j2's AsyncLogger automatically flushes the 256 KB buffer whenever the Disruptor consumer hits endOfBatch (when the queue is momentarily drained), keeping lag in milliseconds.
approachSteps: Explain endOfBatch semantics: if 50 events are queued, Log4j2 writes all 50, then flushes once.
Show that under low load (1 event), endOfBatch=true immediately, so lag is < 1 ms.
Under high load, batching turns 10,800 syscalls into ~32–150 flushes/sec.
tradeOffs: End-of-batch flushing gives both low latency at low RPS and high batching efficiency at high RPS.
failureModes: Setting includeLocation=true in AsyncLogger forces a stack-trace walk on every log call, destroying throughput.

stages.learnerPrompt: A developer enables `includeLocation="true"` (printing class/line number) in the JSON layout. Throughput drops 10x. Why?

referenceMaterial.summary: Capturing caller class/line number requires walking the JVM stack (`StackWalker` / `Throwable.getStackTrace()`) synchronously on the worker thread before publishing to the Disruptor.
approachSteps: Measure stack-walk cost (~15–30 us per log line * 10,800 lines = ~250 ms CPU per second per thread).
Show that location calculation cannot be deferred to the background Disruptor thread.
Disable includeLocation=false and rely on logger name + structured correlation IDs.
tradeOffs: Disabling line numbers removes file:line from logs in exchange for 10x–20x higher logging throughput.
alternatives: Printing stack traces only on ERROR-level exceptions.
failureModes: CPU-bound GC pressure from millions of short-lived StackTraceElement arrays.

stages.learnerPrompt: How do you monitor ring-buffer saturation and disk I/O wait so you catch log storms before they drop ERRORs?

referenceMaterial.summary: Export Log4j2 AsyncLogger RingBufferRemainingCapacity via JMX/Micrometer and alert on Linux node_disk_io_time_seconds_total.
approachSteps: Alert if RingBufferRemainingCapacity drops below 20% of 65,536.
Monitor EBS VolumeQueueLength > 10 or await > 10 ms.
Expose a runtime /actuator/loggers endpoint with auto-revert TTL for temporary DEBUG.
referenceMaterial.codeSnippet:
-- PromQL alerts for log ring buffer and disk saturation
log4j2_ringbuffer_remaining_capacity / 65536 < 0.2
rate(node_disk_write_time_seconds_total[1m]) / rate(node_disk_writes_completed_total[1m]) > 0.01
tradeOffs: Auto-reverting DEBUG log levels after 15 minutes prevents accidental permanent verbose logging.
failureModes: Leaving DEBUG enabled after an incident slowly fills EBS and triggers Fluent Bit backpressure.

spark.summary: Synchronous file appenders with `immediateFlush=true` force every HTTP worker thread to wait on shared `write()` / `fsync()` syscalls, locking up the entire thread pool when EBS IOPS saturate.
spark.keyTakeaway: Switch to Log4j2 AsyncLogger (LMAX Disruptor ring buffer) with batched flushing, `immediateFlush=false`, and `discardThreshold` backpressure so disk stalls never block request threads.

problem.title: Non-Blocking Async & Structured Logging
problem.prompt: A 20-pod Spring Boot order-ingestion service (200 Tomcat worker threads/pod, gp3 EBS 3,000 IOPS limit) enables verbose DEBUG/JSON request logging during an incident. At 1,800 RPS/pod, each request writes 6 log lines (~4.5 KB). With Logback's synchronous `FileAppender` (`immediateFlush=true`), disk queue depth hits 128 and write latency spikes to 45 ms per line—blocking all 200 worker threads in `FileOutputStream.writeBytes` and dropping throughput to near zero.
requirements: Decouple HTTP worker threads from disk I/O so request latency stays < 25 ms even if EBS stalls for 500 ms.
Handle 1,800 RPS/pod (10,800 log events/sec = ~8.1 MB/s) without exhausting JVM heap.
Ensure ERROR/FATAL logs are never silently dropped during normal operation, while gracefully shedding DEBUG/INFO if the disk falls behind.
Keep log-to-disk durability lag under 1 second during normal operation and flush cleanly on SIGTERM.
constraints: Logs must still be written to local `/var/log/app/app.log` for Fluent Bit DaemonSet tailing (cannot switch to direct network-only logging).
Node gp3 EBS volume is shared with containerd image layers and capped at 3,000 IOPS / 125 MB/s.
JVM heap is 4 GB; max memory dedicated to log buffering must be <= 64 MB.

concept.whyItMatters: Logging is supposed to be passive observability, but synchronous appenders put disk syscalls and a global `OutputStream` mutex directly on the request critical path. When a noisy neighbor or verbose log level saturates disk IOPS, every worker thread piles up behind the lock, turning a logging change into a full P0 outage.
whenToUse: High-throughput services (> 500 RPS/pod) writing structured JSON logs to local disk for sidecar/DaemonSet collection.
Cloud VMs or containers backed by burstable/IOPS-capped network block storage (EBS gp2/gp3, Persistent Disk).
Incident scenarios where temporarily raising log levels to DEBUG must not take down production traffic.
whenNotToUse: Financial audit-trail ledgers where every single event must be `fsync`-confirmed to disk before returning HTTP 200 OK.
Low-throughput CLI tools (< 10 logs/sec) where async ring-buffer threads add unnecessary complexity.
keyPoints: Logback's synchronous `FileAppender` acquires a `synchronized` lock around `OutputStream.write()` and flushes every event (`immediateFlush=true`), serializing all 200 worker threads behind disk I/O.

Log4j2 `AsyncLogger` (powered by the lock-free LMAX Disruptor ring buffer) lets worker threads deposit events in ~50 ns while a single background thread batches writes (`immediateFlush=false`, flush on `endOfBatch`).
Always configure non-blocking overflow policies (`AsyncQueueFullPolicy=Discard` for INFO/DEBUG/TRACE) so a dead/full disk sheds verbose logs instead of blocking worker threads.
Use `BufferedOutputStream` (e.g., 64 KB–256 KB buffer) and `AsyncLogger` batching to turn 10,800 tiny `write()` syscalls/sec into ~150 sequential 64 KB writes/sec, slashing IOPS by 98%.
terms: LMAX Disruptor Ring Buffer: Pre-allocated, lock-free circular array using CAS sequence barriers to pass log events from producer threads to a consumer thread with zero GC allocation.
immediateFlush: Appender setting that forces an OS buffer flush after every single log line, destroying batching and multiplying IOPS.
End-of-Batch Flush: Log4j2 optimization that flushes the 256 KB stream buffer only when the Disruptor consumer drains all currently queued events.

tradeOffs.pro: Guarantees HTTP request threads never stall even if `/var/log` is 100% full or EBS hangs.
tradeOffs.con: Can drop DEBUG/INFO logs during a sustained disk outage (mitigated by keeping ERROR/WARN un-discarded up to a safety cap).

tradeOffs.pro: Lock-free CAS ring buffer delivers ~10x higher throughput and zero lock contention vs Logback's `ArrayBlockingQueue`.

failureModes.name: Blocking Async Queue Trap
failureModes.description: Enabling `AsyncAppender` with default `neverBlock=false` (Logback) or `Wait` policy (Log4j2) still blocks all 200 worker threads the instant the buffer fills.

failureModes.name: Gzip Rotation CPU & I/O Spike
failureModes.description: Time/size-based log rotation compresses a 1 GB log file synchronously on the appender thread, stalling writes for seconds.
failureModes.mitigation: Rotate every `100 MB` with `max=5` uncompressed files and let Fluent Bit / logrotate handle compression off-thread.

failureModes.name: JVM Shutdown Log Loss
failureModes.description: Container receives SIGTERM and exits before the background Disruptor thread flushes its 256 KB buffer.
failureModes.mitigation: Ensure Log4j2 shutdown hook runs after Tomcat/Spring graceful shutdown (`shutdownHook=enable`).

commonMistakes: Adding `AsyncAppender` while leaving `neverBlock=false` (default), which still freezes the app when disk is slow.
Leaving `immediateFlush=true` inside an async appender, wasting 90% of the IOPS batching benefit.
Logging full multi-KB request/response JSON payloads at INFO level in hot paths.
Sharing a small 3,000 IOPS EBS root volume across 10 noisy pods without `iops` or `emptyDir` isolation.

sections.content:
## The Problem: 200 Worker Threads Serialized on `writeBytes`

At **1,800 RPS/pod** with `6` DEBUG/JSON log lines per request, each pod generates **10,800 log lines/sec** (`~8.1 MB/s`). Because Logback's `FileAppender` uses `synchronized` locking and `immediateFlush=true`, all **200 Tomcat worker threads** contend on a single monitor lock and issue `10,800` unbatched `write()` syscalls/sec. Across 4 co-located pods on one node sharing a `3,000 IOPS` gp3 EBS volume, write queues hit `128` (`await = 45 ms/line`), locking every HTTP thread and collapsing pod throughput.

## Requirements & Constraints

- **Thread Isolation**: HTTP worker threads must never block on disk I/O (`< 500 ns` log call).
- **IOPS Reduction**: Cut disk write syscalls by `> 95%` at `10,800 events/sec`.
- **Memory & Durability**: Ring buffer `<= 64 MB`; never drop `ERROR` logs during normal load; shed `DEBUG/INFO` if disk stalls.
- **Constraints**: Must write to `/var/log/app/app.log` for Fluent Bit; shared `3,000 IOPS` EBS.

## Ring Buffer & IOPS Math

- **Event Rate**: `10,800 events/sec` at `~750 bytes/event` = `8.1 MB/s`.
- **Disruptor Ring Size**: `65,536` slots (`2^16`) holds **6 seconds** of peak log bursts in memory. At `~750 B` per slot/String, total buffer footprint is `~48 MB` (within the `64 MB` budget).
- **IOPS Savings**: Batching into a `256 KB` `BufferedOutputStream` (`immediateFlush=false`, flush on `endOfBatch`) turns `10,800` tiny writes/sec into `~32–150` sequential writes/sec (`8.1 MB/s / 256 KB ≈ 32` full flushes/sec), cutting IOPS demand by **98.5%**.

data.caption: Replacing synchronous FileAppender with Log4j2 AsyncLogger + Discard policy isolates worker threads from EBS latency spikes.

sections.content:
## Detailed Design: Log4j2 AsyncLogger + Discard Policy

1. **Enable Global `AsyncLogger`**: Add `log4j2-core` + `lmax-disruptor` and set `-Dlog4j2.contextSelector=org.apache.logging.log4j.core.async.AsyncLoggerContextSelector`.
2. **Non-Blocking Overflow**: Set `-Dlog4j2.asyncQueueFullPolicy=Discard` and `-Dlog4j2.discardThreshold=INFO` (drops `INFO/DEBUG/TRACE` when ring is full; never blocks workers).
3. **Batched RollingFileAppender**: Set `bufferSize="262144"` (256 KB), `immediateFlush="false"`, `SizeBasedTriggeringPolicy size="100 MB"`, and `DefaultRolloverStrategy max="5"` without inline `.gz` compression.

## Failure Handling & Edge Cases

- **Pod `CrashLoopBackOff` / OOM**: `AsyncLogger` flushes on `endOfBatch` (every few ms under normal load), so at most ~10 ms of logs are in the 256 KB buffer before crash.
- **Disk 100% Full**: `Discard` policy sheds logs gracefully and increments `discarded` metrics without freezing Tomcat.

## Production Resolution Summary

Migrate from synchronous Logback `FileAppender` to **Log4j2 `AsyncLogger` (LMAX Disruptor)** with `ringBufferSize=65536`, `asyncQueueFullPolicy=Discard`, `discardThreshold=INFO`, `bufferSize=256KB`, and `immediateFlush=false`. Disk IOPS drop by `98%` and Tomcat worker threads never block on EBS.
